articles.title_orig: China accuses US warship of entering waters near disputed Spratly Islands
articles.title_zh: China accuses US warship of entering waters near disputed Spratly Islands
articles.content_orig:
China on Tuesday accused a US warship of illegally entering waters near the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, saying the move jeopardized maritime security and regional stability.
The US littoral combat ship USS Charleston entered waters adjacent to Xianbin Jiao, also known as Sabina Shoal, in China’s Nansha Qundao, or Spratly Islands, early Tuesday without Beijing’s authorization, according to a spokesperson for the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command.
The spokesperson said Chinese naval forces were dispatched to track and monitor the American vessel in accordance with relevant laws and regulations.
“China holds indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters,” the spokesperson said.
The US operation “infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” the spokesperson added.
Beijing urged Washington to immediately halt such operations, warning that Chinese military forces remain on high alert to defend national sovereignty and security.
The spokesperson said the Southern Theater Command would continue safeguarding China’s territorial claims while maintaining regional peace and stability.
The Spratly Islands are claimed in whole or in part by China, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: China opposes US ban on govt agencies from using DeepSeek
articles.title_zh: China opposes US ban on govt agencies from using DeepSeek
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.
The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.
The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.
The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.
Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.
Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.
DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.
The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.
DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.title_orig: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.title_zh: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.title_orig: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.title_zh: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.content_orig:
Shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group plummeted 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, amid a sharp retreat in sentiment towards the sector that has also derailed other planned listings.
Elice, which raised 201.1 billion won ($150 million) in its IPO, provides AI cloud services as well as AI-based education and business software and plans to spend most of its IPO proceeds on launching portable modular data centers and related infrastructure.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether massive AI spending can pay off anytime soon as elevated inflation keeps borrowing costs high.
Analysts noted that Elice's IPO had been priced on Oct. 6, before the recent sell-off in AI-related stocks.
"Elice's debut shows the AI infrastructure trade has moved from 'build at any cost' to 'who is paying and for how long'," said Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based Shenton Research.
"Until the AI labs that rent ... capacity show they can fund their compute commitments, new listings across the region will likely be priced in that risk premium."
This month, data center firms that have shelved their IPO plans include Australia's Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia, Blackstone-backed AirTrunk, which postponed a Singapore REIT IPO, as well as SB Energy, a unit of Japanese tech investment conglomerate SoftBank, which had filed paperwork for a U.S. IPO.
"Everyone is not sure how much demand for AI there will be and it is hard to estimate current demand," added Kim Hak-joon, an analyst at Seoul-based Kiwoom Securities.
Elice's shares were last trading at 63,600 won compared with its IPO pricing of 90,500 won. The IPO drew institutional orders worth 388.84 times the shares available in the offering, according to a filing.
The company has said revenue for the first half of the year tripled to 34 billion won and that it swung to an operating profit of 10 billion won compared with a 3.5 billion won loss for the same period a year earlier.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Pete Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Pete Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections
articles.content_orig:
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.
The meeting between the hawkish ally of US President Donald Trump and the veteran Israeli premier facing a knife-edge election occurred on Monday, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter.
A spokesman for the US Department of Defense told Al Jazeera it “declines to comment” on the report.
Hegseth wrote on a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Asia.
Israel’s Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel’s southern desert.
The reports of the visit come a day after President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
“I endorse American candidates, and that’s where I’m focused on is the midterms,” Vance, who travelled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian elections earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
“I’m not anti-endorsing him, but I’m not pro-endorsing him; I’m not getting involved in Israeli elections,” Vance said.

articles.title_orig: What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car
articles.title_zh: What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car
articles.content_orig:
Australian independent MP Helen Haines is in hospital in a critical condition after she was struck by a car outside her electorate office in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said appears to have been "a deliberate act".
The incident in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, happened on Monday afternoon local time.
Albanese said counter-terrorism police are involved in the investigation.
Haines was struck by a White Toyota Landcruiser outside her electorate office on Monday.
The driver allegedly reversed to run into her a second time, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
"What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time," Burke told national broadcaster ABC on Tuesday morning.
A local barber Ricky Jefferies said he heard a loud commotion and ran towards the car, telling reporters on Tuesday that took a knife off the driver.
He said that multiple people "got involved immediately" to stop the alleged attacker.
Haines was airlifted to a Melbourne hospital where she underwent surgery.
She has lost one of her legs, according to local media. National broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation report that surgeons are working to save her other leg.
Victoria Police arrested the driver of the car, a 43-year-old man from the nearby town of Tarrawingee.
Local media reports have named the suspect as Brendan Nugent. Police have not confirmed the name of the man arrested.
Few details have been shared about Nugent, although he reportedly campaigned widely on environmental issues, including advocating against logging.
He was was detained at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody by officers, police said.
A knife was also seized, according to officers.
Victoria Police said it was unknown whether the suspect and Haines knew each other and its investigation remains ongoing.
On Tuesday morning Albanese said the suspect drove past Haines and did a U-turn "in order to get back" to where she was before hitting her with the car.
"It's clear this was a deliberate act," he told the ABC, adding it was not an "accident".
The motive for the attack is not clear, he said, and police are continuing their investigations.
Haines is a 65-year-old Independent MP for the Indi division in Victoria, south-eastern Australia.
She grew up in the south west of Victoria on a dairy farm with four brothers before training as a nurse and a midwife.
She became the matron of the Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital in Victoria when she was 26, before later completing a master's degree in public health and a PhD in Medical Science while raising her three children and working, according to her website. She lives with her family on a small cattle farm outside Wangaratta.
The MP was first elected to the Australian House of Representatives in 2019 and was re-elected in 2022 and 2025.
Haines's family said the incident happened outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, a city of about 30,000 people, a few hours north-east of Melbourne in the state of Victoria.
Police said she was hit outside an office on Murphy Street at about 15:35 local time (05:35 BST).
Albanese appeared close to tears during a live television interview on ABC's 7.30 programme when he was asked if Australian politicians talk among themselves about the threats and risks they face.
"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one of my colleagues."
He later described how there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Speaking in a news conference, Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there had been an increase in reports of harassing and threatening behaviour towards lawmakers in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with 951 for the previous year.
Paying tribute to Haines during a news conference, Albanese described her as "incredibly hard-working".
"She is fiercely intelligent but most importantly she is just a thoroughly decent human being full of integrity and respected right across the Parliament and from everyone who comes into contact with her", he added.
He said the attack will come as an "incredible shock" to her community.
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the incident as a "shocking and deeply disturbing attack".
The Premier of Victoria Ben Carroll said he was "deeply appalled" by the "violent attack".
Meanwhile, Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the attack.
"This is a shocking day for our nation," he said. "No-one should be targeted in this way."
But MPs from a range of political backgrounds have also described feeling deeply concerned about their safety in recent times: wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.

articles.title_orig: China protests UK border searches, phone seizures amid growing spy claims row
articles.title_zh: China protests UK border searches, phone seizures amid growing spy claims row
articles.content_orig:
Chinese citizens reportedly targeted for questioning under counterterrorism laws, drawing strong response from Beijing
According to a statement from China’s embassy in Britain, multiple Chinese nationals – including trade delegates, tourists and people visiting relatives – have experienced long delays, as well as questioning by Border Force officers and confiscation of phones and other devices.
The embassy said that British border officials claimed their actions were carried out in accordance with relevant provisions of the United Kingdom’s Counterterrorism and Border Security Act 2019.
“China expresses serious concern over this and has lodged solemn representations with the British side,” the embassy said, noting that it would continue to urge Britain to stop the arbitrary detention and questioning of Chinese citizens.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says it's never been so close to Russia after Trump downplayed ties in war
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says it's never been so close to Russia after Trump downplayed ties in war
articles.content_orig:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Russia and Iran have never worked so closely, as Moscow seeks to present itself as a possible mediator in the Middle East war.
Araghchi hosted his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Iran on Monday — the veteran Russian diplomat's first visit to Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes on the Islamic republic at the end of February, sparking the war.
"We covered everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen. Also focused on expansion of economic and nuclear cooperation," Araghchi wrote on X. "Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."
Lavrov said ahead of his visit that Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks stalled between the United States and Iran.
On Sunday, President Trump said in a Truth Social post that "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Mr. Trump has in recent weeks controversially eased U.S. sanctions against Russia , imposed over Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a bid to bring down fuel prices for Americans.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes as President Trump floats resuming military operations against Iran after next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.
Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.
Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.

Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.
"Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."
Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.
Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.
Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.
He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."

articles.title_orig: Gangs in Haiti target foreign troops in the biggest attack since a new force began operations
articles.title_zh: Gangs in Haiti target foreign troops in the biggest attack since a new force began operations
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title_orig: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.title_zh: 'I started ketamine at 14 and needed nappies at 22' - the rise of young people going to rehab
articles.content_orig:
Megan Harmes was 14 when she first tried ketamine.
A decade later, rehab is helping her rebuild her life after bladder issues caused by the drug have left her needing to wear incontinence pads.
The drugs charity Kaleidoscope says it has seen a huge rise in referrals to its detox and rehabilitation facility over the last five years, with two people referred in 2021 compared with 112 so far this year. The majority of clients are aged 18 to 24.
Research is now under way by the University of South Wales into the specific needs of this group, as the harm caused by "chronic, escalating use" of ketamine is far more rapid, over a shorter space of time, than that from alcohol or Class A drugs.
Services traditionally designed for older adults are having to adapt to support much younger people, it said, with very different needs, and habits often formed while they were in school.
For 24-year-old Megan, from Flint in north Wales, drug use became more common among her peers during lockdown.
As an aeronautical engineering apprentice, she was suddenly working from home, on full pay, with access to a drug whose price had plummeted.
She said at its worst, she was on it "all day, every day", according to Megan it helped to suppress symptoms or feelings associated with ADHD and borderline personality disorder.
"I'm very hyperactive now that I'm sober. I haven't been like that since I was 14, it suppressed pretty much everything," she said.
Eventually her ketamine use meant she lost her apprenticeship, causing her to "spiral".
Megan later found work elsewhere, but four years of night shifts further entrenched her use, as she would use ketamine to stay awake through the night even on days off.
For the last two years she has been in agony, unable to stand straight and needing to wear incontinence pads.
"For a 22-year-old wearing pads or nappies, it takes away all dignity," she said.
"Back then I really didn't care whether I lived or died - now I don't want to die.
"I've been in rehab just over four weeks and I'm getting back to my old self."
Megan said she wouldn't know the extent of the damage to her bladder for some time, but she has put on weight and is physically feeling better than when she arrived.
Jo Moore runs the Birchwood rehabilitation facility for Kaleidoscope and said five years ago they had just one referral for inpatient detox from ketamine.
"Since January this year we've seen 112 people come through the door," she said, adding that half their clients are currently being supported for ketamine use.
"It's very, very cheap and very accessible - that's what allows people to use it more frequently and at large amounts at the same time."
The drug is prescribed in healthcare settings as a dissociative anaesthetic, and also used with animals, but was reclassified as a Class B drug in 2014. This means it is illegal to take, carry, make or sell.
Illicit ketamine use among those aged between 16 and 59 in the UK was estimated to be about 264,000 people in 2024-25, with those seeking treatment for ketamine use disorders increasing twelvefold over the course of a decade.
While younger people have driven the rise in its use, Moore said the last year had seen a rise in referrals for adults aged 25 to 34, particularly in Cardiff and south-east Wales.
Dr Darren Quelch, from the University of South Wales, said interviews with service users at Birchwood suggested use started from as young as 13.
He said the physical harm caused by persistent use ranged from memory problems and chronic pain to bladder damage and kidney failure, but that support services were having to rapidly adapt as the needs of users are more complex.
"Their bread and butter isn't dealing with really complex medical presentations," he said. "Even if they were, we actually don't know what the right answer is yet."
He is now conducting research alongside Kaleidoscope to establish what types of support work for this specific patient group.
"The population is inherently different to lots of other groups that might engage with drug and alcohol treatment services," he said.
Mark said his health had deteriorated to such an extent that "at the age of 25 I probably had the body of an 80-year-old".
"I was no longer functioning like a proper human being," he said.
As a keen footballer growing up in Liverpool, he now looks on jealously at others his age, walking without pain.
"It stopped me being a father to the little girl that I've got - I stopped being the big brother, the responsible son," he said.
Mark would regularly pass clots and experience pain during urination, but said the collapse of his nose from snorting drugs has had a huge impact.
"It completely destroys self-confidence - which leads to more drugs, because that just blanked out what I think of myself."
It's one of the reasons he has asked to remain anonymous.
"I started getting looks of disgust from my own family, which destroyed me. It was a very lonely time through my addiction," he said.
Mark's drug use started at 18, but by 21 he said he was using "copious amounts of cocaine and ketamine".
He initially sought help from his GP in Liverpool, but was too ashamed to admit he was using ketamine for fear of being dismissed or judged.
"It's a hard lesson learned," he said.
It's an issue reflected in Quelch's research. He found young people struggled with A&E and GP surgeries, as their symptoms weren't always linked with ketamine use, or the question wasn't always asked.
"That's not necessarily because people aren't asking the right question, but we don't actually know what works well at the moment," he said.
"There's very little provision for young people experiencing drug and alcohol-related harms, and that has almost left us starting right from the beginning."
Moore said things were improving, with greater availability of early intervention in the community, reducing the need for detox.
"We're seeing less people presenting to services with a new substance use of ketamine - so the education in schools, colleges and universities is actually working.
"But we are seeing an increase in people that have been using for a couple of years that we are going to continue to have to help and support."
With trends in drug use evolving, Moore said the challenge for both the third sector and the NHS was to adapt around the needs of clients, but that the involvement of those with lived experience had made a difference.
"I can see improvements now, but there have been some really difficult times where it felt like we were shouting in the dark."
Quelch said, while research continued, the scale of the current ketamine problem was still unclear, as was the longer-term health implications.
"Anecdotally, relapse is a big problem in this group - we don't know the recoverability of their bodies, but we have seen that when people resume using ketamine after a period of abstinence, those harms appear a lot quicker than the first time around," he said.
However, Quelch added the work being done with peer support at Kaleidoscope was "really unique and impactful".
"There was a lack of judgement or stigmatisation - the peer element was really important and is something to learn from the Birchwood environment."
For Mark, it has meant a focus on the future is possible. Like many we spoke to, he was adamant he wanted to give something back.
"I grew up thinking money was everything, but I get joy now from helping other people who are struggling. I was there once and I know how much it means to get someone to help you."

articles.content_orig:
US president says he would welcome three-way discussion on nuclear weapons, but no date or format has been agreed for the proposed meeting
“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation,” Trump told reporters outside the White House before travelling to Kansas. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it.”
“If we can do denuclearisation, I will have done the world a big, big favour,” Trump said, without explaining the scope of any potential nuclear agreement.

articles.title_orig: Bari Weiss Derangement Syndrome
articles.title_zh: Bari Weiss Derangement Syndrome
articles.content_orig:
Phillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on Tuesday
The veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for his CBS News colleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”
Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’s London bureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.
Phillips’s decision to join CBS was announced in June . It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move that shook staff .
The Guardian, which first reported the Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.
Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”
He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, and voiced a short piece on Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.
“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.
He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”

articles.title_zh: Barber says he had 'no choice' but to tackle driver who struck Australian MP Helen Haines
articles.content_orig:
Australian MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese calls "a deliberate act"
The suspect allegedly did a U-turn in order to strike the MP and then reversed to ram her a second time , Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says
The 65-year-old independent MP, who was taken by helicopter to hospital in Melbourne, has reportedly lost a leg
A 43-year-old man, from nearby Tarrawingee, was detained at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody
Police say it was an 'isolated incident' and they are working to identify potential charges
Both MPs and experts have warned that threats to Australian politicians were rising before the Haines incident, writes Tiffanie Turnbull in Sydney
Edited by Helen Livingstone, with Katy Watson in Wangaratta and Lana Lam in Sydney
An outpouring of thoughts and well wishes, in the form of flowers, has built up in the street outside Helen Haines' MP office in Wangaratta this morning.
The tributes illustrate Haines' popularity among members of her electorate.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon says he spoke with Anthony Albanese in the aftermath of the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and passed on "thoughts and prayers from New Zealand".
Speaking to journalists this morning, Luxon described the incident as a âterrible set of circumstancesâ.
"The facts haven't still come out as to what the motivation has been or was, but you know, a concerning development in Australia for sure," he said.
New Zealand's foreign minister Winston Peters said in an X post that "New Zealand is shocked by the attack on Australian MP Helen Haines".
"Violence has absolutely no place in politics," he wrote.
Katy Watson Australia correspondent reporting from Wangaratta
At the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral here in Wangaratta, thereâs a vigil taking place - several hundred people whoâve come to pay their respects and light a candle for Helen Haines who remains in hospital.
âItâs just something that you wouldn't expect in our community,â says Austin Longfild.
âYou see it in other countries and it's just something that I didn't comprehend could happen here, and then it's just happened down the street.â
Heâs full of praise for Helen Haines:

âSeeing how she advocates for the community, she seems pretty authentic,â he says. â©
âWhether you vote for her or not, she seems to have the community actually at heart so thatâs all you can really ask for, for a politician that represents your community.â
Ricky Jefferies says a "lot of people got involved immediately"
Helen Haines, the independent federal MP for Indi, remains in a critical condition in hospital after she was hit by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria, yesterday afternoon.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates.
A man flies the Australian flag outside the office of Helen Haines
Local media are reporting the name of the 43-year-old man arrested yesterday as Brendan Nugent.
It's understood Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was an environmental campaigner with an interest in anti-logging issues.
Nugent was detained by bystanders in the moments after he allegedly drove into Helen Haines outside her electorate office on Monday afternoon.
Haines remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
Katy Watson Australia correspondent reporting from Wangaratta
Helen Hainesâ office is on Wangarattaâs main street, which has now reopened to traffic and cars are slowly filing past.
On the window is a large decal of Dr Haines, smiling at her electorate.
This apparent attack has shocked this small community, and of course the country more broadly.
On the pavement outside her office, thereâs a growing number of bouquets being left for her.
Every so often, another member of the community walks by, stops, and lays another one down.
One card reads "may you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world". Another thanks her for all the "wonderful" work she has done.
We know Helen Haines was taken to hospital with severe injuries to her lower body yesterday, and that she underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a Melbourne hospital.
This morning the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported that the MP has lost one of her legs.
Nine News has also reported this.
The last we've heard from officials is that Haines is in a critical condition.
Fellow
independent MP Allegra Spender has been telling ABC News "many people have feared that there would be some
sort of violent incident against Australian politicians".
"I think this is of
huge concern, because I think we take pride in the fact that in Australia, politicians are just like anybody else, you treat them just like anybody else,
but theyâve got to be accessible, and thatâs really important," she says.
Asked if Australia
has been so far been sheltered from the type of political violence seen towards MPs in the UK, she says âweâve done better in this country, and we have to continue
to do better, and that means in terms of violence against politicians but
frankly - abuse of people in our hospitals, in our supermarkets."
"This is part
of a trend that we I think a country, not just as politicians, we need to step
up and say, we donât want to see this sort of violence in language and
violence in attitude."
"We are collectively responsible for that."
Political leaders have condemned the apparent attack on independent MP Helen Haines who remains in a critical condition in hospital.
Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor says it is a "shocking day for our nation" and that Australians will be "angry and appalled" by the attack.
"Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised," he says.
The Greens leader David Shoebridge says the notion that Haines was targeted for her work is "horrifying, senseless, and shameful".
âWe cannot let political violence become the norm and I believe that politics grounded in non-violence is a powerful way to address this threat.
And Senator Pauline Hanson , leader of One Nation, says: "Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia".
Steve Manning, the independent candidate for Ovens Valley, in north-east Victoria, says that a vigil will be held for Helen Haines in Wangaratta this afternoon.
Manning told Australia's national broadcaster, the ABC, that those who wished to take part should come to the Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral at 1pm local time.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) Commissioner has just released a statement about Helen Haines with an update on the 43-year-old man who was arrested shortly after the incident.
The AFP and Victoria Police are "working closely together to identify potential charges," says Krissy Barrett, with possible state and Commonwealth offences including causing harm to a public official which carries a maximum penalty of ten years in prison.
"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are no known threats connected to this matter," she says.
The investigation is being led by Victoria Police's security investigation unit with support from the state's joint counter terrorism team, which is includes the AFP and ASIO, Australia's spy agency.
Federal police have regularly raised concerns about "growing threats against federal parliamentarians and high office holders," Barrett says, and last October, a special unit was established to probe politically-motivated violence and hate, with 41 people charged as a result.
The head of Australia's intelligence services, Mike Burgess, has issued a statement warning that increased levels of "grievance, intolerance and polarisation continue to create a permissive environment of violence" in Australia.
He says that the agency, ASIO, is concerned about the "use of violent rhetoric in public discourse".

articles.title_zh: General Motors is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what Wall Street expects
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors is set to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell Tuesday.
Here is what Wall Street is expecting, according to average estimates compiled by LSEG:
Those results would mark relatively flat revenue compared with a year earlier and a roughly 30% increase in adjusted earnings per share. GM's 2025 third-quarter results included $48.59 billion in revenue, net income attributable to stockholders of $1.3 billion and earnings per share of $2.80 adjusted.
Investors will be watching to see if GM raises its 2026 guidance and for any early indications of expectations for next year, which Wall Street expects will be difficult for the U.S. automotive industry.
"While we expect in-line to slightly better 3Q26 prints, investor focus is likely to be on 2027 revisions and we don't see results driving meaningful upside," JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta said in an Oct. 11 investor note.
Wall Street analysts are mixed on whether GM, which has regularly raised guidance during the year, will do so Tuesday amid concerns of slowing sales and rising commodity costs.
GM raised its 2026 forecast when reporting second-quarter results to include adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $14 billion and $16 billion, or $12 and $14 adjusted EPS. Its forecast for adjusted automotive free cash flow is between $9.5 billion and $11.5 billion.
Aside from results and guidance, investors will be watching for updates on the company's launch of redesigned full-size pickup trucks , its warranty improvements and any notable growth in GM's software and service operations.

articles.title_orig: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.title_zh: China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
articles.content_orig:
Model marks shift from R&D to commercialisation and aligns with country’s effort to cut reliance on imported tech
China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan.
Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market.
This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from research and development to commercialisation, according to a report by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily on Monday.
It also represents the latest achievement aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on imports of the technology used in vital advanced industries like chip manufacturing.

articles.title_orig: ‘Deliberate’ car ramming of Australian MP an isolated incident, police say
articles.title_zh: ‘Deliberate’ car ramming of Australian MP an isolated incident, police say
articles.content_orig:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have said the alleged targeting of independent lawmaker Helen Haines appeared to be an “isolated incident” and there were no known further threats associated with the attack.
Haines was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her office in Wangaratta, about 200km (124 miles) northwest of the state of Victoria’s capital, Melbourne, on Monday, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a “deliberate” act.
The 65-year-old underwent surgery overnight, with Australian media outlets reporting on Tuesday that she has lost a leg and remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
The suspect is in police custody, an AFP statement released on Tuesday said. Local media identified the driver as a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, Victoria.
Federal and state police were working “to identify potential charges”, including “the offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment”, the statement said.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that the vehicle had performed a U-turn before hitting the MP.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone just skidding off the road,” Albanese ⁠told the ABC national broadcaster.
The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown.
A former nurse, Haines is an independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi and is known for her socially conscious policy positions on the environment and transparency.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC Radio that witnesses said Haines was struck twice by the vehicle before a bystander intervened.
Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restrained the attacker and removed a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported.
“I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy; I just ran out to the ⁠front to see what’s happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop.
“I didn’t realise the seriousness of ⁠the situation initially, and once it became relevant, I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.”
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was shocked by the “deeply disturbing attack” and wished Haines a full recovery in a post on X.
The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.
Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
She has been praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

articles.title_orig: 5 Cheaper OLED TVs To Buy Instead Of The Samsung S95H
articles.title_zh: 5 Cheaper OLED TVs To Buy Instead Of The Samsung S95H
articles.content_orig:
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Samsung's S95H, which is referred to as S99H in Europe, is the company's 2026 flagship OLED TV. It has received wide acclaim for its picture quality, and even recently swept all the best TV awards in HDTV's 2026 shootout . The TV is available in four sizes in the U.S. and has much to like, from its vibrant QD-OLED display panel (except the RGB Tandem OLED panel in the 83-inch model) to impressive gaming features, including a 165Hz refresh rate. However, being a flagship OLED TV, it has a hefty price tag, with a list price ranging from $2,500 for the 55-inch model to $6,500 for the 83-inch variant.
If you're looking for a good OLED TV , you don't necessarily need to pay top dollar for the S95H. There are mid-range and entry-level models from not only Samsung, but also brands like LG, Roku, Sharp, and Sony that you can consider. Generally, each OLED TV offers fantastic picture quality, but you may have to sacrifice brightness, gaming features, and other aspects. We have carefully selected some of the best yet affordable OLED TV models to help you get started. We've considered expert reviews and user feedback, whenever available.
If you're set on getting a Samsung TV, which is reasonable considering it has the best customer satisfaction rating among major smart TV brands , but don't have the budget for the S95H, the company's S85H OLED TV is worth considering. It's significantly more affordable, starting at $1,200 for its 48-inch model. More importantly, as we are heading into the holiday season, discounts are only expected to increase. You can also choose from five different screen sizes, from 48 inches to 83 inches.
Unlike Samsung's S95H, which uses a QD-OLED panel for most of its sizes, the S85H relies on a WOLED panel. It also has a 4K resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate with VRR. Other features include support for HDR10+ and Dolby Atmos. Unfortunately, there is no Dolby Vision support . The TV runs on Tizen with One UI, which provides access to popular streaming services, Samsung TV Plus, Google Cast, Apple AirPlay, and more. Additionally, one little detail that separates Samsung OLED TVs from other manufacturers is that Samsung is set to provide seven years of OS upgrades , which is uncommon in this industry.
Experts from Rtings.com , Tom's Guide , Trusted Reviews , and WhatHiFi are happy with the S85H's performance and highlight its sleek design and image processing. However, they aren't too fond of the audio quality, stutter in slow-panning shots, and its limited reflection handling. The TV has garnered an average buyer rating of 4.1 out of 5 on Amazon, with shoppers liking the picture quality and easy unboxing. That said, some buyers don't appreciate the TV setup process, calling it "unbelievably difficult" and "awful."
Sony doesn't really have a track record of offering affordable OLED TVs , but this year, the company is offering the Bravia 6 as an entry-level model, which can be a good choice for anyone not looking to spend the big bucks. It comes in a wide range of sizes, from 48 inches to 83 inches, giving you plenty of choice. It also has a starting list price of $1,300, but it has started getting listed at a discount.
The Sony Bravia 6 runs on Google TV, which offers access to popular smart TV apps , Google Cast, and much more, including the Gemini AI assistant. In other highlights, the TV comes with a 120Hz refresh rate with variable refresh rate (VRR), and support for Dolby Vision HDR, Dolby Atmos, and DTS:X. All of its four HDMI ports support full version 2.1 bandwidth, and one is eARC-compatible. The TV also has a built-in ATSC 3.0 tuner. Other connectivity and port options include two USB-A ports, one of which is rated for 5 Gbps speeds and 4.5W of power output, Wi-Fi 6E, an Ethernet port, and optical audio out.
The one thing Sony TV lovers will miss from the Bravia 6 is the company's proprietary XR co-processor, and a MediaTek chip is responsible for all the image processing. As a result, it's not as good as other Sony TVs at content smoothing. Still, it does do a pretty good job. Experts from Rtings.com like its picture quality and performance. However, they note it has a hard time reducing glare in bright rooms. Buyers on Amazon have also given it a rating of 4.3 out of 5 and are happy with its gaming features and visual performance. The only concerns some Amazon shoppers have are its relatively lower overall brightness and slow startup time.
Another Samsung TV that you can consider is the S90H . It sits between the S85H and S95H in Samsung's portfolio and is significantly closer to the S95H in terms of the feature set than many of our other recommendations. It's available in a ton of sizes, ranging from 42 inches to 83 inches. Notably, Samsung is using different OLED panel technology in different sizes. For example, 42-inch, 55-inch, 65-inch, and 83-inch models have a regular WOLED panel, whereas 48-inch and 77-inch models come with newer RGB Tandem OLED panels. RGB Tandem OLED panels typically deliver better performance than WOLED panels. Another highlight of the display panel is the matte coating, which helps in countering glare and reflections.
The S90H has a 4K display with a 165Hz refresh rate, which high-end gaming PC owners would certainly appreciate. It also comes with four HDMI 2.1 ports, each of which can handle a 4K 165Hz signal, three USB ports, 3.5mm audio out, optical audio out, and Wi-Fi 6E. Moreover, you get HDR10+ support and Dolby Atmos, but there is no Dolby Vision or DTS audio support, like the S85H.
The S90H starts at a list price of $1,400 for the 42-inch model, but goes up to $5,300 for the 83-inch model. However, it's increasingly available with significant discounts. The TV has received glowing reviews from CNET , IGN , Rtings , T3 , and Wirecutter experts, who like its strong gaming support, anti-glare screen, and picture quality. However, there are some concerns about its low-resolution content smoothing quality and the lack of Dolby Vision support. Amazon shoppers also have a positive opinion of the TV and have given it a good average buyer rating of 4.4 out of 5. The only notable complaints are about the user interface of the TV.
The B6E is the cheapest OLED TV you can find in LG's 2026 lineup. It has a starting list price of $1,400 and is available in 55-inch, 65-inch, and 77-inch models. However, if you time your purchase correctly, you can get it for almost half price. Like our other recommendations, it has a 4K resolution and comes with a 120Hz refresh rate panel with support for VRR. It also supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos. Moreover, LG has included four HDMI 2.1 ports, Wi-Fi 5, one USB-A port, an Ethernet port, and optical audio out. The built-in tuner is, however, limited to ATSC 1.0, and you get a simple remote that lacks motion controls or a microphone.
Like other LG TVs, the B6E runs on the webOS platform, which has all the popular apps. Rtings.com experts have good things to say about the B6E and praise its feature set and performance, including low-quality content upscaling; however, they highlight the lack of support for DTS audio formats as well as stutter in slow-panning visual shots. Best Buy shoppers have awarded the TV an excellent buyer rating of 4.7 out of 5, and note that the TV offers excellent picture quality and solid gaming features. That said, some buyers aren't happy with LG's smart TV OS, which feels cluttered.
You can also consider the LG B6 if you are willing to shell out a bit more. It's largely the same TV as the B6E but comes with LG's Magic Remote and advanced features like room audio correction, AI voice recognition, and SDR-to-HDR upscaling. Moreover, the B6 comes in 48-inch, 65-inch, 77-inch, and 83-inch sizes.

articles.title_orig: French riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates
articles.title_zh: French riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Looting and rioting across France over the weekend are threatening to reshape the contours of the French presidential race.
Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seizing on the crisis to cast herself as the candidate of law and order, but there are risks for her too. Many voters see her as a highly divisive leader whose 2027 victory would only deepen the societal fault lines exposed by the riots.
Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, widely tipped to challenge Le Pen in the second round next year, is also treading carefully as rivals accuse him of encouraging the rage on the streets that has morphed into pillaging and arson.
For the flailing centrists, there is now an opportunity to finally make an impression in the contest — but only if they can distance themselves from President Emmanuel Macron, who is seen as fluffing his response to the nationwide wave of vandalism.
Overall, it’s pushing the election into uncharted waters.
“If there’s a real crisis, you don’t know where it could lead,” said one conservative who holds regular talks with officials from the far-right National Rally and was granted anonymity to discuss the subject.
Where does that leave the candidates? POLITICO takes a look at the strategic calculus for the leading runners across the political spectrum.
Le Pen is receiving an immediate boost. Even her rivals admit it.
This Saturday’s unrest “benefits the far right,” said center-right European Member of Parliament Nathalie Loiseau. “They are circling around the violence like vultures,” she said in an interview.
Le Pen has already cast herself as the alternative president, delivering a sober address to the nation Sunday and pitching herself as the candidate of a “ pacified France .”
Jordan Bardella, president of her National Rally party, upped the ante on the protests and pitched his party as the only one able to restore order, dialing up fears about the pillaging. The rioters “will soon be breaking into people’s homes,” he said at a press conference in Paris. “The authorities are collapsing.”
But excessive, prolonged chaos could backfire on a party long seen as instigating civil unrest. And the topic is already becoming a talking point inside the National Rally.
“Some say that this shows that there will be riots if the National Rally comes to power,” said Charles-Henri Gallois, one of Bardella’s advisors. “But I don’t believe it.”
According to the conservative quoted above, periods of instability can lead the French to turn their backs on anti-establishment figures and prefer traditional veterans.
“You could end up with [Charles] De Gaulle on the Champs-Élysées,” the official said, referring to how the first president of the Fifth Republic emerged with extra powers after the 1958 crisis that roiled the nation.
Far-left leader Mélenchon is in a bind as he walks a tightrope between supporting protesters and distancing himself from violence.
The France Unbowed party supported the school protests in the run-up to last weekend’s riots, and far-left elected officials have played a prominent role in the blockades, either in decrying alleged police violence or in support of the protesters.
In the battle for leadership between Mélenchon and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, the former grabbed the limelight.
But the violence this weekend could end up marginalizing the far left, especially with the government and political rivals accusing them of fueling the unrest. “They tried to aggravate the situation,” Loiseau said.
According to a poll from Cluster 17 for POLITICO, the 75-year-old far-left firebrand is already one of the most commonly “rejected” politicians in France.
On Monday, Mélenchon tried to turn the tables, firing back at the government, saying the prime minister was fomenting “disorder” with his accusations that ultra-left groups were trying to disrupt the election.
For the center-right presidential hopeful Philippe, the riots aren’t good news either. He has to work hard to distance himself from his old boss, President Emmanuel Macron, who is seen as failing to respond sufficiently to the crisis. (Philippe was Macron’s first prime minister.)
But the protests could also be his opportunity to show some character, and rebut critics who think his campaign lacks energy and panache . Philippe, the best-placed centrist candidate to beat the far-right, has seen his poll ratings stall in recent months and has struggled to cut through the campaign noise.
A break with Macron might just be what he needs.
Philippe came out hard against the president after he failed to announce any measures during his primetime television address Sunday. “I would have preferred… decisions and initiatives to restore order,” he wrote online. “This country needs someone in command.”
But the former PM will need to stick his neck out more if he’s going to make an impact.
“He’s very presidential, and it’s a posture that suits him,” said one of Macron’s ministers, who, like others cited here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly.
“But he’s not saying anything. What’s his measure? Why doesn’t he say we need to call a state of emergency? “
For the MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, the protests are a trial by fire after he won the Socialist Party primary contest earlier this month and became the center-left’s presidential candidate.
On Monday, Glucksmann tried to strike a very different note from Mélenchon, telling reporters that “it’s unbearable … that hordes of looters should attack symbols of the state.”
Sensing a chink in the far-left leader’s armor, he accused the leader of France Unbowed of being “a springboard” for Le Pen, who would be “the beneficiary of the chaos.”
Glucksmann has seen his poll ratings go up since he won the Socialist Party primary outright, reaching 15% to 16.5% according to a recent Elabe poll — in a similar territory to Mélenchon and Philippe.
But the minister quoted above expected Glucksmann to peak soon.
“He can only take voters away from Mélenchon,” the minister said. “A left-wing voter may vote for the right, but a right-wing voter won’t vote for the left anytime soon,” the person said.
Macron is being roasted for going on television to address the nation and announce … absolutely nothing.
On Sunday, Macron promised that rioters who “destroyed” things would have to pay the price and called for “clear answers” on why the protests turned violent.
“Fucking hell, it’s rubbish,” said one former senior government official.
Macron has cultivated an image of being above the fray and went on a trip to the Middle East on Monday. But his failure to respond to the violence risks damaging his final months in power. “It’s out of touch,” a regional official said.
According to the minister quoted above, Macron should have let his prime minister do the talking but instead was encouraged to make “a speech to calm” the situation.
On Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu tried to get a grip on the situation, announcing localized curfews, movement restrictions, and bans on public demonstrations.
But another day of demonstrations has already been announced for next Saturday, sparking fears the protests will snowball into sustained protests similar to the Yellow Vests movement in 2018 and 2019.
If so, this chaos will be a defining element of the 2027 campaign.
